parts.label: a
parts.body: Identify two trends observed in human evolution from the data in the table.

rubric.criterion: Any 2 of the following trends (1 mark each, max 2 marks): Progressive increase in cranial capacity/brain size from Australopithecus to Homo sapiens
Progression from semi-upright to fully upright/bipedal posture
Progression from no tools to increasingly sophisticated/complex tools
Change from herbivorous to omnivorous diet
Development from simple lifestyles to complex social organisation and technology

example_answer.content:
Two trends observed:
1. There is a progressive increase in cranial capacity from Australopithecus afarensis (400–500 cc) to Homo sapiens (1350–1450 cc).
2. There is a progression from no tools or crude stones to increasingly sophisticated tools and technology.

parts.label: b
parts.body: State the significance of the development of an omnivorous diet in human evolution.

rubric.criterion: An omnivorous diet allowed hominids to exploit a wider range of food sources/resources.
This increased chances of survival, especially when specific food types became scarce.
It also allowed colonisation of diverse habitats/environments.

example_answer.content: The development of an omnivorous diet was significant because it allowed hominids to exploit a much wider range of food sources, including both plant and animal matter. This greatly increased their chances of survival, especially during times when specific food types were scarce, and enabled them to colonise diverse habitats and environments.

parts.label: c
parts.body: Explain the advantage of an upright (bipedal) posture in human evolution.

rubric.criterion: Upright/bipedal posture freed the hands/forelimbs for other activities such as making and using tools, carrying food, and caring for young;
It also elevated the head, improving the visual field/ability to see predators and prey from a distance;

example_answer.content: The development of an upright (bipedal) posture was advantageous because it freed the hands for other activities such as making and using tools, carrying food, and defending against predators. It also elevated the head, providing a better visual field for spotting predators and prey from a distance.

parts.label: d
parts.body: Suggest why Homo sapiens has been more successful than earlier hominids.

rubric.criterion: Homo sapiens has the largest brain/cranial capacity, enabling higher intelligence, advanced reasoning, problem solving, and creativity; This led to development of language, culture, sophisticated technology, agriculture, and complex social structures, giving Homo sapiens a superior ability to adapt to and modify the environment;

example_answer.content: Homo sapiens has been more successful than earlier hominids because of its significantly larger brain, which enables higher intelligence, advanced reasoning, and creative problem-solving. This has led to the development of language, complex social structures, agriculture, and sophisticated technology, giving Homo sapiens an unparalleled ability to adapt to and modify virtually any environment on Earth.

questions.body: Explain how each of the following provides evidence for organic evolution.

parts.label: a
parts.body: Fossil records.

rubric.criterion: Fossils show a record of organisms that lived in past geological periods.
By studying fossils in different layers of sedimentary rock, scientists can trace how organisms have changed over time from simpler to more complex forms.
Older/simpler fossils are found in deeper/lower layers while more recent/complex fossils are in upper layers.

example_answer.content: Fossil records provide direct evidence of organisms that lived in the past. Fossils found in sedimentary rocks show that organisms have changed over time, from simpler to more complex forms. Older fossils in deeper rock layers tend to be simpler, while more recent fossils in upper layers are more complex. This progression documents the gradual change in life forms over millions of years.

parts.label: b
parts.body: Comparative embryology.

rubric.criterion: Early embryos of different vertebrate classes (fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds, mammals) are remarkably similar in appearance.
Shared features include gill slits/visceral clefts, tail buds, segmental muscle blocks (myotomes), and a single circulation.
These similarities suggest that these organisms share a common ancestor from which they diverged.

example_answer.content: Comparative embryology reveals that the early embryos of different vertebrate classes — fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds, and mammals — are remarkably similar, sharing features such as visceral clefts (gill slits), segmental muscle blocks (myotomes), and a single circulation system. These striking similarities in early development strongly suggest that all vertebrates descended from a common ancestor.

parts.label: c
parts.body: Cell biology.

rubric.criterion: All eukaryotic cells have common organelles such as membrane-bound nuclei, mitochondria, ribosomes, and Golgi bodies.
Green plants share chloroplasts and cellulose cell walls.
These cellular similarities across diverse organisms indicate a common origin/ancestry.

example_answer.content: Cell biology shows that all eukaryotic cells share common organelles including membrane-bound nuclei, mitochondria, ribosomes, and Golgi bodies. Similarly, all green plants possess chloroplasts and cellulose cell walls. These cellular similarities across vastly different organisms indicate that they share a common evolutionary origin.

rubric.criterion: If there were no variations, all individuals would be identical/genetically alike and would respond to environmental changes in the same way;
If the environmental change was unfavourable, no individual would have an advantage over others/none would be better adapted;

The entire population could be wiped out/become extinct because there would be no individuals with favourable traits to survive and reproduce in the new conditions; Natural selection would have no variation to act upon;

example_answer.content: If there were no variations in a population, all individuals would be genetically identical and would respond to environmental changes in exactly the same way. If the environment changed drastically in an unfavourable direction, no individual would have any advantage over the others — none would be better adapted to the new conditions. Consequently, the entire population could be wiped out and become extinct, because there would be no individuals with favourable traits that natural selection could act upon to ensure survival and reproduction in the changed environment. This illustrates why genetic variation is essential for the survival and evolution of species.

questions.body: Explain what would happen to a population of organisms if there were no variations among the individuals and the environment changed drastically.

rubric.criterion: Homo sapiens has a much larger cranial capacity (1350–1450 cc) compared to Australopithecus (400–500 cc)
Homo sapiens is fully bipedal/upright while Australopithecus was semi-upright
Homo sapiens has a flatter face/reduced jaw and brow ridges compared to the more prominent jaw and brow ridges of Australopithecus
Homo sapiens makes and uses sophisticated tools and technology while Australopithecus used no tools or only crude stones
Homo sapiens has a well-developed capacity for speech/language while Australopithecus had limited communication
Homo sapiens is omnivorous while Australopithecus was mainly herbivorous
Homo sapiens has a more complex social organisation and culture
Homo sapiens has an opposable thumb that is more refined for precise tool use

example_answer.content:
1. Homo sapiens has a much larger cranial capacity (1350–1450 cc) compared to Australopithecus afarensis (400–500 cc), indicating greater brain size and intelligence.
2. Homo sapiens is fully bipedal with a fully upright posture, while Australopithecus afarensis was only semi-upright.
3. Homo sapiens makes and uses sophisticated tools and technology, while Australopithecus afarensis used no tools or only crude stones.
4. Homo sapiens has a well-developed capacity for speech and language, while Australopithecus afarensis had very limited communication abilities.

questions.body: State four ways in which Homo sapiens differs from Australopithecus afarensis.
(a) State the meaning of the term 'gene pool'.

parts.label: b
parts.body: Explain how mutations contribute to evolution.

rubric.criterion: Mutations are random changes in the DNA/genes of an organism; They introduce new alleles/genetic variations into the population/gene pool;

If a mutation produces a favourable trait, the individual possessing it has a survival advantage through natural selection and passes the new allele to offspring; Over time, the frequency of the beneficial allele increases in the gene pool, leading to evolutionary change;

example_answer.content: Mutations are random, spontaneous changes in the DNA sequence of an organism's genes. They introduce new alleles into the gene pool, increasing genetic variation within the population. If a mutation produces a trait that gives an individual a survival or reproductive advantage in its environment, natural selection will favour that individual. It will survive, reproduce, and pass the new allele to its offspring. Over successive generations, the frequency of the beneficial allele increases in the gene pool, driving evolutionary change.

parts.label: c
parts.body: Distinguish between a gene mutation and a chromosomal mutation.

rubric.criterion: A gene mutation is a change in the nucleotide/base sequence of a single gene/DNA molecule.
while a chromosomal mutation involves a change in the structure or number of entire chromosomes (e.g. deletion, duplication, inversion, translocation, polyploidy).

example_answer.content: A gene mutation is a change in the nucleotide (base) sequence within a single gene on a DNA molecule, such as a substitution, insertion, or deletion of one or a few bases. A chromosomal mutation involves a change in the structure or number of entire chromosomes, such as deletion of a chromosome segment, duplication, inversion, translocation, or changes in chromosome number (e.g. polyploidy).

questions.body: (a) Explain the concept of 'survival of the fittest' using an example of organisms in a changing environment.

parts.label: b
parts.body: A population of bacteria is exposed to an antibiotic. After several rounds of treatment, a strain of bacteria emerges that is completely resistant to the antibiotic.

rubric.criterion: (i) Within the original bacterial population, there was genetic variation; Some bacteria possessed mutations/genes conferring resistance to the antibiotic;
(i) When the antibiotic was applied, susceptible bacteria were killed but resistant ones survived (natural selection);

(i) The resistant bacteria reproduced and passed on resistance genes to offspring; After several rounds of treatment, virtually all surviving bacteria were resistant, forming a fully resistant strain;
(ii) Any 2 of the following precautions (1 mark each, max 2 marks): Always complete the full prescribed course of antibiotics

example_answer.content:
(ii) Two precautions to reduce antibiotic resistance:
1. Always complete the full prescribed course of antibiotics to ensure all bacteria, including partially resistant ones, are killed.
2. Only use antibiotics when prescribed by a qualified medical professional and never use them for viral infections, to avoid unnecessary exposure of bacteria to antibiotics.

parts.label: i
parts.body:
Explain how this resistant strain evolved.
(ii) State two precautions that can be taken to reduce the development of antibiotic resistance.

questions.body: Give the meaning of the following terms as used in evolution.

parts.label: a
parts.body: Adaptive radiation.

rubric.criterion: Adaptive radiation is the evolution of many different species/forms from a common ancestor, each adapted to a different environment/mode of life/ecological niche; Accept: A form of divergent evolution where a single ancestral species diversifies into many species occupying different habitats;

example_answer.content: Adaptive radiation is the evolution of many different species from a single common ancestor, each adapted to exploit a different environment or ecological niche. For example, Darwin's finches on the Galápagos Islands evolved from a single ancestral species into many species with different beak shapes adapted to different food sources.

parts.label: b
parts.body: Continuous variation.

rubric.criterion: Continuous variation is variation in which there is a complete range of measurements/values from one extreme to another with no distinct categories; It is controlled by many genes (polygenic) and influenced by the environment; Examples: height, weight, skin colour;

example_answer.content: Continuous variation is a type of variation where characteristics show a complete, unbroken range of values from one extreme to another with no distinct categories. It is controlled by many genes (polygenic inheritance) and is influenced by the environment. Examples include height, weight, and skin colour.

parts.label: c
parts.body: Discontinuous variation.

rubric.criterion: Discontinuous variation is variation in which individuals fall into distinct/separate categories with no intermediates; It is usually controlled by one or a few genes and is not influenced by the environment; Examples: blood group, tongue rolling ability, sex;

example_answer.content: Discontinuous variation is a type of variation where individuals fall into distinct, separate categories with no intermediate forms. It is usually controlled by one or a few genes and is largely unaffected by the environment. Examples include blood group (A, B, AB, O), ability to roll the tongue, and sex (male or female).

questions.body: A population of moths in a forest includes individuals with light wings and individuals with dark wings. The forest has trees with light-coloured bark.

parts.label: a
parts.body: Which wing colour gives a moth a survival advantage in this forest? Explain your answer.

rubric.criterion: Light-winged moths have a survival advantage; because they are camouflaged against the light-coloured bark and are less easily seen/detected by predatory birds;

example_answer.content: The light-winged moths have a survival advantage in this forest because their light colour camouflages them against the light-coloured bark of the trees, making them less visible to predatory birds.

parts.label: b
parts.body: A factory is built near the forest and over time, soot darkens the tree bark. Predict and explain the expected change in the proportion of light-winged and dark-winged moths after many generations.

rubric.criterion: After soot darkens the bark, dark-winged moths would be better camouflaged against the dark tree trunks and would gain a survival advantage; They would be less visible to predators, survive longer, reproduce more, and pass on their genes;
Light-winged moths would become conspicuous on dark bark and would be more easily preyed upon, decreasing in number;
Over many generations, the proportion of dark-winged moths would increase while the proportion of light-winged moths would decrease;

example_answer.content: After soot from the factory darkens the tree bark, the dark-winged moths would become better camouflaged against the dark trunks and would gain a survival advantage — they would be less easily detected by predators, survive longer, and reproduce more. In contrast, the light-winged moths would become conspicuous against the dark bark and would be easily spotted and preyed upon by birds. Over many generations, the proportion of dark-winged moths in the population would steadily increase, while the proportion of light-winged moths would decrease.

parts.label: c
parts.body: Name the specific example of natural selection in moths that this scenario is modelled on.

rubric.criterion: Industrial melanism in the peppered moth (Biston betularia);

example_answer.content: Industrial melanism in the peppered moth (Biston betularia).

questions.body: (a) Explain the importance of variation in the process of natural selection.

parts.label: b
parts.body: State three sources of genetic variation in organisms.

rubric.criterion: Any 3 of the following sources (1 mark each, max 3 marks): Mutation — random changes in DNA/genes introduce new alleles

example_answer.content:
Three sources of genetic variation:
1. Mutation — random, spontaneous changes in DNA introduce new alleles into the population.
2. Crossing over — during prophase I of meiosis, homologous chromosomes exchange segments of genetic material, creating new allele combinations.
3. Independent assortment — during meiosis, homologous chromosome pairs orient randomly at metaphase I, producing gametes with different combinations of chromosomes.

parts.label: c
parts.body: Explain why organisms produced by asexual reproduction are more vulnerable to environmental changes than those produced by sexual reproduction.

rubric.criterion: Organisms produced by asexual reproduction are genetically identical/clones of the parent; They have little or no genetic variation;

If the environment changes unfavourably, all individuals are equally susceptible and the entire population could be wiped out/become extinct; In contrast, sexually reproducing organisms have greater genetic variation, increasing the probability that some individuals possess traits suited to the new conditions and will survive;

example_answer.content: Organisms produced by asexual reproduction are genetically identical clones of the parent organism, meaning they have little or no genetic variation. If the environment changes unfavourably (e.g. a new disease or drastic temperature change), all individuals are equally susceptible because none has an advantageous variation, and the entire population could be wiped out. In contrast, organisms produced by sexual reproduction have much greater genetic diversity, increasing the likelihood that some individuals will possess traits suited to the new conditions and will survive.

rubric.criterion: The wings of a bird are made of bones covered with feathers, while the wings of an insect are thin membranous structures without bones; They have different embryonic origins/basic structures;
Despite their different structures and origins, both types of wings perform the same function of flight; They are therefore analogous structures;

This is an example of convergent evolution — the two unrelated organisms independently evolved similar structures for the same function due to similar environmental selection pressures (need for flight), supporting the theory that evolution occurs through adaptation to the environment;

example_answer.content: The wing of a bird is a forelimb made of bones (humerus, radius, ulna, carpals, metacarpals, phalanges) covered with feathers, while the wing of an insect is a thin, membranous extension of the exoskeleton with no bones. Although these wings have completely different embryonic origins and structural compositions, they both serve the same function — flight. They are therefore analogous structures. This is an example of convergent evolution, where two unrelated organisms have independently evolved similar structures to adapt to similar environmental demands. This provides evidence for evolution by showing that natural selection can produce similar solutions to the same environmental challenge in completely different organisms.

questions.body: Explain how comparative anatomy of wings of a bird and wings of an insect provides evidence for evolution.

rubric.criterion: Resistant mosquitoes possess genes/mutations that enable them to survive exposure to the insecticide;
When the insecticide is applied, resistant mosquitoes survive while susceptible ones are killed; The resistant ones reproduce and pass on the resistance genes to their offspring (natural selection);
Over successive generations, the population becomes predominantly resistant, and the insecticide is no longer effective in killing them; A different insecticide or control method must be used;

example_answer.content: Resistant mosquitoes carry genes (often arising from mutations) that enable them to survive exposure to the insecticide. When the insecticide is applied, it kills the susceptible mosquitoes but the resistant ones survive. Through natural selection, the resistant mosquitoes reproduce and pass on their resistance genes to their offspring. Over successive generations, an increasing proportion of the mosquito population carries the resistance genes. Eventually, the population becomes predominantly resistant, and the insecticide can no longer effectively control them. At this point, a different insecticide or alternative control method must be employed.

questions.body: Explain why mosquitoes that have developed resistance to a particular insecticide are difficult to control.
(a) State the role of isolation in evolution.

parts.label: b
parts.body: Name four types of isolation mechanisms that prevent interbreeding between populations.

rubric.criterion: Any 4 of the following types (1 mark each, max 4 marks): Geographical/physical isolation

example_answer.content:
Four types of isolation mechanisms:
1. Geographical (physical) isolation — physical barriers such as mountains, oceans, or deserts separate populations.
2. Ecological (habitat) isolation — populations live in different habitats within the same geographical area.
3. Temporal (seasonal) isolation — populations breed or are reproductively active at different times.
4. Behavioural (ethological) isolation — differences in mating behaviours or courtship rituals prevent interbreeding.

parts.label: c
parts.body: Explain why geographical isolation is considered one of the most important mechanisms leading to speciation.

rubric.criterion: Geographical isolation is important because physical barriers (mountains, oceans, rivers, deserts) can completely prevent gene flow between large populations over very long periods of time;

The separated populations experience different environmental conditions and selection pressures; Over long periods, they accumulate sufficient genetic differences through natural selection and mutation to become reproductively incompatible, forming distinct species (allopatric speciation);

example_answer.content: Geographical isolation is considered one of the most important mechanisms leading to speciation because physical barriers such as mountain ranges, oceans, and deserts can completely block gene flow between large populations for millions of years. The separated populations experience entirely different environmental conditions and selection pressures. Over such long time periods, they independently accumulate sufficient genetic differences through natural selection, mutation, and genetic drift that they become reproductively incompatible even if the barrier is later removed. This process, called allopatric speciation, is thought to account for the majority of new species formation.

rubric.criterion: Ability to rationalise/higher thinking capacity/advanced brain/higher intelligence
Ability to walk on two legs (bipedalism), freeing the hands for tool use
Ability to communicate through speech/language
Opposable thumbs for precise grasping and manipulation
Binocular/stereoscopic vision for depth perception
Ability to make and use sophisticated tools and technology

example_answer.content:
1. Humans have a highly developed brain with advanced thinking and reasoning capacity, enabling problem-solving, creativity, and complex social organisation.
2. Humans have the ability to communicate through speech and language, allowing the transmission of knowledge across generations.

questions.body: State two advantages that humans have gained over most other animals as a result of evolution.

rubric.criterion: Similar blood pigments such as haemoglobin are found in widely different animal groups — e.g. haemoglobin is found in all vertebrates and also in annelids (earthworms);
The presence of the same type of conjugated protein/pigment in such diverse organisms indicates that they evolved from a common ancestor/have a common origin;

example_answer.content: Similar blood pigments, such as haemoglobin (a conjugated protein with an iron-containing prosthetic group), are found in widely different animal groups. For example, haemoglobin is present not only in all vertebrates (fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds, and mammals) but also in some invertebrates such as earthworms (annelids). The presence of the same type of oxygen-carrying pigment in such diverse organisms strongly suggests that these different animal groups share a common evolutionary ancestor.

questions.body: Explain how the presence of similar blood pigments in different animal groups provides evidence for a common origin.
